en.name: *Maria Theresa with Sons Below the Bust of Her Deceased Husband Franz Stephan of Lorraine and Chancellor Kounic-Rietberg*
en.justification: Empress Maria Theresia and her eldest son, emperor Joseph II, were very much engaged in reforming the absolutist reign towards a more responsible one, and did successfully improve the social, economic and administrative conditions of their dominions.

Guided by enlightened reformist ideas, Emperor Joseph II, the eldest son of the empress Maria Theresia, was engaged, like his mother, in improving the social, economic and administrative conditions of their dominions.

For an administrative building in the Moravian capital, Brno, it was planned to celebrate the reign of the Austrian Habsburg-Lorraine imperial dynasty as a victory of reason. An oil-study for the main ceiling fresco shows the pagan god Apollo at the centre bringing a flame as the symbol of enlightenment to the female personification of Reason. Antiquity is presented as the Golden Age of mankind and the heyday of philosophy.

The empress Maria Theresia of Habsburg and her husband emperor Frances of Lorraine reigned beneath Germany, Bohemia and also Hungary in the rank of kings. The triumphal arch of Vác, designed in a severe classical style, and in terms of its formal roots, the rational style, commemorates the imperial visit of 1764.

Economic growth was the main motivation behind the Austrian empress Maria Theresia’s support of Dutch merchants who then founded the Privileged Society for Sugar Production. Their factory in Rijeka, Croatia, produced enough sugar for the entire monarchy so that sugar could be exported widely to other countries, among which was even the Islamic Turkish empire.

Attempts by enlightened sovereigns to improve the economy not without concurrently respecting the worker’s social needs was adopted by the European nobility who often established manufactories to guarantee, or raise, their own incomes. An example of this is seen in the street with lodges for craftsmen, which was provided by the owners of Villa Ghisilieri near Bologna.

In the Augustinian monastery at Polling, one ceiling fresco in the library hall commissioned by the erudite provost Franciscus Töpsl is a statement to the main principle of the Enlightenment: that the truth should be “unveiled” with the help of reason.

In the Jesuit church of Zagreb, the traditional topic of Saint Catherine’s dispute with pagan philosophers was no longer used to degrade profane science against theology, but was now used to plead for the unification of both as equal sources of human wisdom. The illusionistic painted architecture of the high altar is the solemn setting for this enlightened statement.

en.name: The faculty of natural sciences
en.justification: The integration of the natural sciences in the educational and research programmes of the ecclesiastical institutions was the main topic of the enlightened era. In the ceiling of the great hall at the high school in Eger (so-called Lyceum) are paintings of the four traditional faculties being watched over and lit up by God. Under them, Science is portrayed occupied in typical activities.

A good example of an ecclesiastical scientist of the enlightened era is the famous Croatian Jesuit, Ruđer Bošković, who was teaching mathematics and related natural sciences in Rome. His portrait shows him self-confidently handling the typical instruments of his profession: a pair of compasses and an armillary sphere.

en.name: Library
en.location: Ephiscopal Cathedral and Bishop's Palace, Kalocsa, Bács-Kiskun County
en.justification: During the enlightened era, science and erudition took on new value for ecclesiastical institutions in the Catholic sphere. Renewals and upgrades of libraries can be observed everywhere in Europe and can be seen, for example, in the bishopric palace of the Hungarian town Kalocsa.

The exterior of Vác Cathedral is an outstanding example of an austere Neoclassicism typical of the enlightened era. The combination of the portico motif (which was borrowed from antiquity) and simple block-like geometric shapes was intended to re-introduce rationality to church architecture after it had waned during the heyday of the Baroque.

Szombathely Cathedral combines obvious Baroque traditions of church architecture with the new enlightened taste of Neoclassicism and Louis XVI-style decoration. The latter brings with it a reduction of ornament through which the interior obtains its classicising touch. Simple architectural motifs in red marble, especially the columns, give the space a rational structure.

The triumphal arch of 1764 commemorates the visit of empress Maria Theresia, also the Queen of Hungary, together with her husband Francis of Lorraine, to the Hungarian town of Vác. While the building style refers to antiquity and the Roman Empire, and with that is implied its power, the austere block-like and only modestly decorated architecture seems typical of the rationality of enlightened Neoclassicism.

The painter of the ceiling frescoes inside the Servit church in Tyrolean Volders was the well-known Martin Knoller who had been trained at the Academy of the Nude in Rome under the guidance of the classicist pioneer, Anton Raphael Mengs. His well-drawn figures, which were studied accurately by using life models, are very good examples of a conscious rational representation of the human form during the enlightened era.

The assembly of three saints depicted by the Bolognese painter Ubaldo Gandolfi is a good example of the severe classicising academicism of the enlightened era. Anatomically-correct figures are combined together in a composition only suggestive of a holy conversation. The academic study of the nude was often done in relation to antique statues. It is known that Gandolfi was a member of the Clementine Academy in Bologna.

In the enlightened era, sculptures followed antique examples. The academically-trained Moravian sculptor, Gottfried Fritsch, is portrayed together with a statue made of white marble. It remains unclear whether the pair of compasses in his hand indicates that he is measuring an antique figure in order to study it or whether he is in the process of one of his own works concerned with the correspondence of the antique proportional system.

After 1754, for the traditional Hofburg in Innsbruck, empress Maria Theresia commissioned a new stretched façade which was upheld in a modest Roman Baroque style because the building had to serve as an imperial residence in the capital of her dominion Tyrol.

The huge ceremonial hall of the Hofburg in Innsbruck (so-called Hall of Giants) was newly decorated under the reign of emperor Joseph II, between 1773 and 1776, in a moderate Rococo style. The ceiling fresco visualises the conditions of the Habsburg reign.

The higher-ranking nobility concurred with the representational and cultural modes of the Habsburg sovereigns. As distinct from their courtly, moderate Rococo style, the enlightened state chancellor Václav Antonín Kaunitz-Rietberg, in his residence in Austerlitz, preferred classicising Louis XVI decorations.

The higher-ranking nobility concurred with the representational and cultural modes of the Habsburg sovereigns. At Esterháza the noble Hungarian family Esterházy imitated the imperial summer residence in Schönbrunn near Vienna to contain an enlightened cultural life.

In the 18th century in Bologna the Institute of Sciences was founded, which was very important for developing the new concept of scientific studies based on practice and experiments. The original, preserved wax cabinet with its precise models allowed study of human anatomy.

As an enlightened patron of the arts and erudition, the noblemen, traveller and collector, Count Aloisio Ferdinando Marsili, promoted the Institute of Sciences and the Academy of Fine Arts, the so-called Academia Clementina, in Bologna. The lapidary Latin inscription of the epitaph praises only these two actions among all the count’s other merits.

Enlightened promotion of education and erudition in Hungary is highlighted by the high school of Eger, the so-called Lyceum. The erudite and business-minded Bishop Károly Esterházy, who was educated in Rome, commissioned for this purpose a palace-like building, which was crowned by the tower of a well-equipped astronomical observatory. At the nucleus of the noble interior is a huge library.

The pharmacy is a reconstruction of an 18th-century apothecary, with its numerous niches and shelves painted in creamy grey and the detailing in gold. The shelves are lined with examples of Portuguese pharmaceutical earthenware of the period. Inside the old pharmacy is the pharmaceutical arsenal used in the preparation of medicines.

In the enlightened-era, academies of fine arts played a more and more important role in training artists. The Moravian sculptor Gottfried Fritsch is portrayed with a pair of compasses in his hand, and therefore, as a learned artist using scientific methods in measuring and understanding the human form. It is known that Fritsch studied at the academy in Vienna.

The secret societies of freemasonry, the so-called lodges, needed special rooms for their assemblies. In these rooms, which were often decorated with typical symbols, the members celebrated an enlightened cult of wisdom by performing mysterious rituals.

The parish church of the former Benedictine abbey Wessobrunn was erected at the beginning of the enlightened era in Bavaria. Its Baroque architecture sets the scene for the interior decoration in the fashionable Rococo-style, but the clear narrative iconography seen in the ceiling fresco follows enlightened tendencies.

en.name: The Assumption of the Virgin Mary – Presbitery rotunda
en.location: High altar and dome of the choir, Benedictine abbey and pilgrimage church of the Holy Virgin Mary
en.justification: In the 1780s the Benedictine monks of Ettal commissioned a new interior decoration for the rounded presbytery of the abbey church. The new classicising taste of the enlightened era stands in stark contrast to the rich Rococo decoration of the main domed rotunda. A Baroque feature that remains is the iconographic connection between the altarpiece and the ceiling fresco showing the Assumption of the Virgin Mary.

Although erected during the heyday of the enlightened era, the parish church in the Tyrolean village, Weer, operates with true Baroque effect: an illusionistic painted dome provides the setting for a historical scene referencing the life of the holy patron, and the liturgical furnishing is also in the Baroque tradition. The decoration, however, leans more towards the ornamental Rococo style than it does to the classicism of the enlightened era.

Decorated in the classicising Louis XVI style, the Tyrolean parish church in Brixen im Thale – called the “peasant’s cathedral” because of its huge size – represents a rare example of the enlightened search for clarity and noble simplicity in art and architecture. Despite this, the high altar stands typologically in the tradition of Baroque models, although with reduced ornamentation. The lack of any eccentric features, such as curving of the entablature or accumulation of columns, gives it a classical appearance.

The exterior of the parish church of the Hungarian town Papa, erected 1774–86, presents an obvious mixture of Late Baroque building traditions and elements of Neoclassicism. Inside one finds a similar mixture of Late Baroque church furnishing and Louis XVI-style decoration. The iconography of the ceiling frescoes is mostly in the narrative style of the enlightened era.

Inside the church of the Premonstratensian abbey Nová Říše in Moravia, illusionistic architecture in the Baroque tradition (but executed in 1766) provides the framework for narrative paintings which follow the enlightened principle of clarity and ease of understanding. The picture on the high altar is surrounded by a carved frame in the ornamental Rococo style.

The famous statesman and prime minister of Portugal, Marquis de Pombal, became the major figure for the reconstruction of Lisbon after the 1755 earthquake. In the foreground are the plans for a college founded by him to educate the nobility according to enlightened values.

After the 1755 earthquake, the centre of Lisbon (the so-called Lower Town) was reconstructed by following the rectangular raster system. Three monumental squares contained highlights of the town’s architecture inside an overall urban rearrangement. The series of two-levelled arcades and the geometrical and repetitive façades are based on enlightened principles of rationality and simplicity.

After the 1755 earthquake it was necessary to repair the monumental aqueduct that brought water from a spring named *Belas Águas Livres* to the centre of Lisbon. Proposed in 1723, and begun in 1731 under the auspices of the king, it is the result of a responsible reign with due attention to the population’s needs during the enlightened era.

The urban raster system, despite having been developed in earlier times, found its highpoint in the enlightened era because of its geometrical simplicity and rationality. For example, it was also used in Croatia (former part of the Hungarian kingdom) to rearrange the city of Bjelovar in 1771 after the fortifications were demolished.

Social responsibility as a political aim had its roots in the proto-enlightened times of the late 17th century. In the 1690s in Rome, for example, the Popes initiated a huge hospital for poor and old people as well as for youths from impoverished backgrounds and abandoned children. Especially the so-called correction building, created by Carlo Fontana for the treatment of criminal boys and young men, soon became the worldwide prototype for prison architecture.

The so-called Spanish Steps were an important urban intervention of the popes in Rome during the enlightened era. Leading up from Piazza di Spagna to the church of Trinità dei Monti, construction of the steps was seen as a necessity to link important lower- and higher-level areas of the city. A commemoration plaque emphasises, therefore, that public convenience was the main purpose of building the steps.

The erection of a new communal opera house in Bologna shortly after the mid-18th century, was a public affair and, therefore, is a good example of the higher-ranking citizens’ interest in musical culture during the enlightened era. The wooden model was presented to the public as a preview of what was envisaged.

In about the mid-18th century, the world-famous soprano castrate Carlo Broschi, called Farinelli, was portrayed by the Spanish court painter Corrado Giaquinto. Giaquinto depicts himself in the background as the draughtsman. The portrait came into being during the heyday of the enlightened era, and Farinelli’s adoption of a nobleman’s attitude to signal self-confidently his status as a venerated opera star, is in keeping with the mood of the era.

During the enlightened era, erudition was more and more claimed as an important female attribute. This portrait from the second-half of the 18th century, shows a finely dressed and learned noblewoman holding a pair of compasses in her hand and sitting amidst sheets of drawing paper, a ruler and a protractor. At the time, geometry was considered as an acceptable form of entertainment for amateurs and, therefore, was seen as part of a good education.

Without any pathos, but looking self-confident, a woman celebrates a symbolic sacrifice in front of a statue representing Cupid to commemorate her marriage. Her elegant costume and the Neoclassical ambience breathe the spirit of the Enlightenment as well as the sensual melancholy of the scene.

The so-called “fête champêtre” (countryside feast) genre, represented here by an Italian example, came into vogue in 18th-century Europe. This phenomenon is an expression of an awakening sensuality for the pleasures of nature that are to be found at the countryside and the yearning which is connected with that.

An aristocratic couple depicted as Adam and Eve sitting in the Garden of Eden represents a very unusual and bizarre example of the portrait genre: their nakedness contrasts in the extreme with their white wigs, which conform to 18th-century fashion. As a statement about enlightened thinking the travesty of the biblical scene is reclaimed to comment on the supposed free will of the first human couple because of their acting independently of God's wish. Above all, it was the famous French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–78) who created a philosophy propagating the natural condition of the human being as the expression of an ideal mental and social liberty.

The interior of the parish church in Götzens is splendidly decorated with all the overcrowding typical of the full Rococo style. Despite that, the topics of the fresco cycle are selected due to the educational principles of Enlightenment: scenes taken from the Bible, such as the History of the Apostles, should instruct the faithful in living an exemplary Christian life.

en.name: *Life of St John Baptist*
en.location: Ceiling of the nave, Parish church of St John Baptist
en.justification: Inside the Bavarian parish church in Wessobrunn a single fresco covers the entire ceiling of the nave, telling in several scenes the life of the church’s holy patron. While the narrative iconography is taken from the Bible and told according to enlightened educational principles, the perspective employed in the illusory, pompous architecture of the rear scene, obviously belongs to the Baroque tradition.

en.name: *Conversion of St Paul*
en.location: Ceiling of the nave of the Premonstratensian abbey church St Peter and Paul, Nová Říše, Moravia
en.justification: A dramatically composed historical scene, dedicated to one of the church’s holy patrons, telling of the shocking spiritual conversation of the apostle St Paul, dominates the main vaulting of the abbey church in Moravian Nová Říše. The huge fresco brings the message of the scripture abruptly to the fore in the minds of the faithful. In an enlightened sense, therefore, allegory was not employed to distract the viewer from the rationale behind the image.

In this historical painting of about 1795/6 the artist’s endeavour to achieve realistic scenery is remarkable; the faces are lively too, and the costumes are painted in great detail. The enlightened aim towards historical truth is perceptible despite the fact that it has all sprung out of an artist’s imagination. A deliberate feature of the painting is seen in the costumes, which are not medieval but contemporary, and symbolise the continuity of the Cistercian foundation from the past to the present.

Toward the end of his career, the famous Austrian painter, Franz Anton Maulbertsch, drafted this scene of the visitation between the Virgin Mary and her female cousin, Elizabeth, for the high altar of Szombathely Cathedral. According to the enlightened principles of education the clear figural composition should ensure that the faithful would easily recognise and understand the depicted topic while the genre-like accessory figures in the foreground could help the viewer to get into the spirit of the picture.

The ceiling fresco above the entrance hall of Villa Borghese, painted in the 1770s, shows primarily the defence of Rome by the republican hero, Furius Camillus, observed from heaven by Romulus, the mythical founder of the city. Typically for the enlightened era, history is brought to the foreground while allegory is reduced to the well-known symbols of the pagan gods and two figurative groups left and right. The latter mean the eternality of time and the changing, but at least fortunate, fate of Rome.
